conflict_topics: ventilation responsibility / who must ventilate when cooking
whether a standing rule should require ventilation when cooking
dialogue_quality_notes: Participants made concrete, verifiable actions (extractor turned on, stove released, utensils washed, stove taken) which grounded the dialogue.
Agent A offered a temporary practical concession while refusing a retroactive blanket rule — realistic trade-off language.
Agent C's repeated request to label utensils is functionally useful and not merely repetitive; there is minimal needless restatement.
Environmental state updates are consistent and helpful to track progress.
evaluation.final_reason: Immediate practical issues were addressed: Agent A turned on the extractor, finished cooking, washed utensils and freed the stove (resolved in round 2), and Agent D began cooking. Agent A labeled her own utensils (partial progress). The substantive normative dispute about a standing ventilation rule and who bears responsibility (and the related practical question of moving the drying rack/window opening) remained unresolved through the end.
position_change_notes: Agent A retained opposition to a retroactive blanket ventilation rule but softened position by turning on the extractor, washing utensils, freeing the stove, and agreeing to discuss rules later (evidence: Turns 1, 3, public updates).
Agent B continued to insist on shared expectations about ventilation but accepted the immediate extractor use; B's normative demand remains unaccepted (Turn 2).
Agent D requested stove access and obtained it without contest after Agent A released the stove (Turns 7-8, public updates).
Agent C consistently sought clarity about utensil ownership; Agent A labeled her own utensils, but other occupants did not label theirs by the end (Turns 5, 18-19).

round_scores.evidence: Agent B demanded immediate ventilation and a standing rule; Agent A refused a retroactive blanket rule but agreed to turn the extractor on for five minutes and finish the dish. Agent A physically turns on the extractor. (Turn 1, Turn 2, public update)

Agent A removes the dish, washes shared utensils, frees the stove and agrees to keep the extractor on until smell's gone, while saying 'We can talk later about a lasting rule.' The future-rule disagreement remains unresolved but immediate practical conflict is reduced. (Turn 3, Turn 5, public updates)

Agent D takes the stove to begin cooking and Agent A agrees; extractor remains on and aroma is fading. The standing-rule/ventilation responsibility issue remains unaddressed but no new substantive conflict occurs. (Turn 7, Turn 8, public update)
Two more minutes pass with extractor on and window closed; no one advances the unresolved issue about a future ventilation rule or who must move laundry if window opened. (public update)
Another two minutes pass with the same physical state (extractor on, window closed, laundry exposed). The unresolved normative question about ventilation responsibility persists. (public update)

Agent C repeats a request to label personal utensils; Agent A labels her own utensils now but cannot label others'. This partially reduces the shared-objects ambiguity but leaves other occupants' labeling and the ventilation/rule issue unresolved. (Turn 18, Turn 19, public update)

substantive_insights: Immediate practical conflict (stove access, odour mitigation, dirty shared utensils) was resolved through short-term, task-focused concessions rather than agreement on norms.
There is a persistent tension between a cook's responsibility to ventilate and the practical risk (rain on drying laundry) that makes a simple rule contested during incidents.
Partial compliance (Agent A labeling only her own utensils) reduces uncertainty but does not fully solve the shared-ownership problem without reciprocal actions from others.

normalizations: Removed resolution_round 2 because the final status is partially_resolved.
